thesis: Unspent gift card money is not grabbed when a card goes quiet: companies predict from their own history how much will never be spent and book that share as sales, a little at a time.
centralQuestion: Who keeps the money on an unspent gift card?

conflict.wants: The store wants revenue it can count on; the holder wants their balance.
conflict.obstacle: Cards that never expire can't simply be taken back.
conflict.stakes: Starbucks booked $222.4 million this way in one year.

misconception: The store takes the money when a card expires.
originalAngle: The company's own filing explains the forecast in one line; most explainers stop at 'stores profit from forgotten cards'.

hookCandidates.text: In the US, Starbucks cards don't expire. Its latest annual report still counts $222.4 million of card money as sales, and no drink was served for it.
Look at the gift card in your drawer. The company that sold it has already estimated how likely you are to spend it.
Who keeps the money on an unspent gift card?
A gift card is money the store owes you. Some of that debt slowly turns into the store's sales.
Starbucks booked $222.4 million in its latest fiscal year from card money it doesn't expect to see redeemed.

questions.text: Who keeps the money on an unspent gift card?

payoff: The store keeps the predicted share, a little at a time; part can go to the government; the rest is still yours to spend.
